1:
This chapter is the same hymn as the eighteenth psalm in a different recension, and that fact governs almost everything the commentary says about it. Clarke states the consequence bluntly: since the substance and almost the words are the same, the exposition must be reserved for the psalm, and he confines himself to a very few observations. Ellicott instead makes the comparison his whole method, and begins where the difference begins: the psalm's opening line, in which the singer declares that he will love the Lord his strength, is wanting here though it forms a fitting introduction to the whole, and the omission is partly compensated by the words about refuge and saviour and deliverance from violence which stand here and not there. He notes that the two expressions the psalm keeps separate, my God and my rock, are here united in one, and that the recurrence of the same united phrase near the end of this chapter but not of the psalm shows the change was intentional. Delitzsch sets out the architecture rather than the variants, taking the opening verses for an introduction containing the sum and substance of the whole, in which David groups the many experiences of deliverance in his agitated life, before the first half pictures that deliverance as an extraordinary theophany and then unfolds its ground.

Who is speaking is the chapter's deepest question, and Clarke raises it by way of a long citation rather than in his own voice. The poetry is universally admired, runs the argument he reproduces, and yet cannot be perfectly understood until it is known who the speaker is, who the person triumphant over mighty enemies, whose sufferings occasioned such a convulsion of nature, and who on his deliverance inflicted such vengeance on his own people and became a king over the heathen. Should we be told the person was David, it is very difficult to show how the description can agree with that character; and if it did agree it would contradict the apostle, who quotes part of it as predicting the conversion of the Gentiles. If the speaker is David only, the Messiah is excluded. From the difficulties on either side the general idea has been that it relates to both. Clarke's own position is firmer than that: though in a primary sense many of these things belong to David, generally and fully they belong to the Messiah alone.

On the titles Henry is fullest, reading them as a series of answers to particular distresses. All others adored as deities are counterfeits and pretenders, for they are dead while the Lord lives and they disappoint their worshippers when most needed; men begin in kindness but do not end, promise but do not perform, whereas God will finish his work and his word is tried. From the single confession that he is my God Henry derives the rest: then my rock, the shelter which is as the shadow of a great rock in a weary land and the rock on which hope is built; my fortress, in which I am safe and think myself so; my high tower, out of reach of real evils and neither to be scaled nor battered nor undermined. Am I in distress, he asks, then God is my deliverer; struck at, my shield; pursued, my refuge; oppressed, my saviour; and more, the horn of my salvation, by which I am strongly protected and my enemies strongly pushed. On the cry out of distress Delitzsch renders the strophe as breakers of death compassing him about and streams of wickedness terrifying him, with cords of hell girding him and snares of death overtaking him; and Ellicott notes that where the psalm has the bands of death this chapter has the waves, an entirely different word whose variation can hardly have been accidental and which accords better with the parallelism of the next clause.
8:
The theophany is where the two texts diverge most, and Ellicott catalogues the divergences as evidence rather than curiosities. Where this chapter has the foundations of heaven shaken, the psalm has the foundations of the hills; the thought is the same, he says, but the strong figure by which the mountains are called the pillars of heaven is softened in the psalm. Where this chapter says the Lord was seen upon the wings of the wind, the psalm says he did fly, two words exceedingly alike in the Hebrew and either easily mistaken for the other, the psalm's being far the more poetical. In the verse about darkness a word appears to have dropped out here, since the psalm has the fuller reading about a secret place and a pavilion of dark waters, and in the second clause Ellicott prefers the margin's gathering of waters, which differs from the psalm's word by a single letter. He would also read out of the brightness rather than through it. From the several slight differences in this passage he draws his general conclusion, that they mark the two as distinctly different recensions, and notes as the most striking change the shift of the final pronoun from his to thy in the psalm, as appropriate to its use in public worship.

Delitzsch works the same ground with a harder instrument. In the opening strophe he finds that the received vowel reading obliterates a significant alternation between two verbal forms, that foundations stands here in the feminine plural, and that where the psalm has the mountains this text has the heavens by an extension of the figure, meant not of mountains holding the sky up but of the points of support of the heavens themselves, so that the whole universe trembles. Of the verse about the brightness he says flatly that it is terribly mutilated, only four letters surviving of the clause the other text preserves. Where the text stands he reads it as weather: the splendour of the divine nature, enveloped in clouds, breaks through the dark covering in burning coals of fire, which are the lightning that shoots from the storm-clouds. On the deliverance strophe he weighs three variants and finds one unimportant, one less pleasing in language and rhythm, and one a clumsy emphasising of the pronoun.

Clarke stops for one verse only, and for a reason neither of the others gives. In the line about riding upon a cherub he finds sense and sound astonishingly well connected, and sets out the Hebrew word by word so an unlearned reader may hear it, observing that the clap of the wing and the rush through the air are expressed in a very extraordinary manner. Henry declines the textual question and asks instead why the language of Sinai is used at all, since we do not find that in any of David's battles God fought for him with thunder as in Samuel's time, or with hail as in Joshua's, or with the stars in their courses as in Deborah's. He gives four reasons. The metaphors set forth the glory of God, whose wisdom and power and faithfulness appearing for David were as clear a discovery to an eye of faith as miracles would have been to an eye of sense; his displeasure, since he so espoused David's cause that he showed himself an enemy to all his enemies; the confusion his enemies were thrown into, as if the earth had trembled and the foundations of the world been discovered; and his readiness to help, hastening to David's succour though he had seemed at a distance, and making darkness his pavilion for the amazement of his enemies and the protection of his own. On the close Henry fastens on the reason given, that the deliverance came not from common providence but from covenant love: he delivered me because he delighted in me.
21:
Here the psalm turns from deliverance to its ground, and Delitzsch is at his most severe on the text. In the strophe pleading righteousness he notes that the form used for my righteousness here and again later is contrary to the usage of the Psalms, and that a poetical construction found in Job has been replaced by a common prose phrase. In the next strophe he reports a reading for which there is no example elsewhere, since the usual expression for innocence speaks of the hands, and a verb form which has only the sound of the reflexive it appears to be, being really a reflexive of another stem after the manner of Aramaic. At the verse about the lamp he finds a word lost outright, since the divine name is called light in the Psalms but not lamp, the spelling of the surviving word wavering incorrectly between two forms, and the repetition of the divine name by which the loss is covered inelegant. At the verse about gentleness he says the five-line stanza is stunted by the falling away of its middle line, which in the psalm runs that thy right hand supported me.

Ellicott traces the same divergences without the asperity, twice preferring the psalm on poetic grounds. Where this chapter has the singer not departing from the statutes, the psalm by a very slight change has him not putting the statutes away from himself; the former is the commoner form, he says, the latter suits the parallelism here better. Where this chapter has my cleanness the psalm has more poetically the cleanness of my hands. Where this chapter has thou art my lamp, the psalm changes the figure to thou wilt light my candle. For unsavoury he would read froward, since although the form here is anomalous it is the same word bearing the same reference as in the psalm; for God is my strength and power he would read my strong fortress, noting that the psalm has quite a different thought here which this chapter expresses several verses later; and on thy gentleness he agrees with Delitzsch that the word here differs very slightly from the psalm's and is otherwise unknown, so that taken as it stands its etymology would make it thy answering to the prayers offered. He adds that the psalm inserts the missing line between the two clauses.

Henry reads the section as a question of what the deliverances were for, and finds the answer in the enlargement that followed. God sometimes brings his people into very great difficulties, he says, that he may have the honour of saving them and they the comfort of being saved by him; and the deliverance is magnified by the greatness of the danger, since the singer was surrounded with death on every side and could no more help himself than a man in the grave can. The successes are then a second mercy on the first, for God had not only preserved but prospered him: he was brought into a large place where he had room to thrive, and his steps were enlarged under him so that he had room to stir, no longer straitened and confined. From the plea of integrity Henry takes his own improvement of the relation rather than a defence of the claim: if God be mine then in him will I trust, resigning myself to his direction and depending on his power and wisdom and goodness, and on him will I call, for he is worthy to be praised; what we have found in God worthy to be praised should engage us both to pray to him and to give glory to him. On the lamp he puts the figure as question and answer: am I in the dark, benighted, at a loss, then thou art my lamp to show me my way, and thou wilt dispel my darkness.
38:
Through the victories Delitzsch keeps finding the same kind of loss, and they are losses of art rather than of sense. Where the psalter has the singer overtaking his enemies, this text has him destroying them, by which, he says, the echo of the song at the sea is obliterated; and the following clause about consuming them he calls tautological after the words before it. The two figurative expressions about the dust and the mire appear here, in contrast with the other text, in a distorted form. At the verse about the heathen he judges the variant right in referring the contentions to those within David's own kingdom, and finds the corresponding variant about being kept for a head reasonable and in harmony with it. At the doxology he notes that the change of position of the divine name is against the rhythm, and the shortened verb both against the rhythm and contrary to custom; and he traces how the word here has been corrected from one form into another to yield the tower of salvation, a figure recalling the psalms and the proverbs. The one word he calls troublesome is the rock thrust into the verse about the living Lord.

Ellicott reads the same divergences as mostly scribal, once as designed. The destroying for overtaking is meant to suggest the same thing as the plain expression here, while the former of the two clauses about consuming is wanting in the psalm and the latter needs a stronger word, crushed. Where this chapter has they looked, the change of a letter makes it they cried in the psalm, and the Greek renders it so here too; one reading, he says, is doubtless a clerical error. The same verdict covers thou hast kept me against the psalm's thou hast made me, a mere clerical variation. But the dust is different: the psalm reads dust before the wind and omits the second clause here about spreading them abroad, so combining in one compact figure what this text spreads out in two, and that change, Ellicott judges, is certainly designed and heightens the poetic effect. He notes that two clauses are transposed between the texts, and ends on the finest variant: the verbs differ by the transposition of a letter, so that where the psalm has the conquered coming trembling from their fastnesses, this text has them coming limping, suggesting the remnant of the enemy had already been injured and wounded.

At the close the two voices part on what the comparison has shown. Ellicott makes it a lesson in providence: the brief review of the two recensions is instructive, as showing that Providence has dealt with the manuscripts of the Old Testament as with those of the New, securing them through a long succession of ages from all substantial error, and yet not so overruling ordinary human action but that mere slips of the pen should creep in and care and diligence be required to establish what was originally written, the smallest details sometimes remaining uncertain. The psalm itself he calls a grand anthem of thanksgiving for the many mercies David had received, a full and confident expression of trust under all circumstances and of well-assured hope in the promised perpetuity of his kingdom through the coming of him in whom all the families of the earth should be blessed. Henry ends on the publicity of the praise rather than the text: to him will I give thanks, and that publicly, for among the heathen David would neither be afraid nor ashamed to own his obligations to the God of Israel. The titles Henry opened the psalm with he closes it with as well: the Lord is the horn and the rock of salvation, his saving strength being in him and from him, and the tower of salvation can never be scaled nor battered nor undermined, since salvation itself saves him.
